segments.t: On a quiet Parisian street, Andrea intercepts Hicham during his morning jog to deliver shocking news. Hesitant to meet casually, she reveals that she is pregnant with his child and needs to talk. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Qu'est-ce que tu fais là, Andréa?
Je dois te demander quelque chose.
On peut boire un verre ensemble?
Je devais absolument te le dire.
Now let's break down the scene step by step. Listen to each line, followed by its meaning and a short explanation.
Qu'est-ce que tu fais là, Andréa?
'What are you doing here, Andrea?' Literally 'what is it that you do there?', this handy sentence is the standard French reaction when bumping into someone unexpectedly.
'Wait just one little minute.' Slipping 'little' ahead of 'minute' is a classic French softener — the same touch you'll hear in 'a little coffee' for 'a quick coffee'.
'I am doing my last lap.' That closing word — familiar in English from cycling's famous 'Tour' — simply means a 'lap' or 'loop' in French.
Je dois te demander quelque chose.
'I must ask you something.' Notice where 'you' sits in French: it tucks right ahead of 'to ask' rather than after it or before 'must'.
On peut boire un verre ensemble?
'Can we have a drink together?' Literally 'drink a glass', this three-word expression is the go-to invitation in French for grabbing a drink.
'Why should we see each other?' Putting 'ourselves' ahead of 'would see' gives the reciprocal meaning 'see each other' in French.
'To talk calmly, that is all.' Adding '-ment' onto 'calm' works just like adding '-ly' in English, closed off by the handy chunk 'that is all'.
'Do you want to seduce me again?' Where English saves 'again' for the end, French places it right after 'want' — literally 'you want again me to-seduce?'.
'No, that is not true!' Because 'not' steps in front of 'is', contracted 'it's' expands back into full 'that' at the start in French.
'I am pregnant, Hicham.' French uses a dedicated word here that looks nothing like English 'pregnant' — never swap in 'full', which applies only to animals!
'What? Are you really serious?' Speaking to Andrea, 'serious' swaps its silent '-x' ending for '-se', which you'll hear pronounced with a clear 'z' sound.
Je devais absolument te le dire.
'I absolutely had to tell you.' Where English leaves 'it' unspoken after 'tell you', French stacks both 'to-you' and 'it' right ahead of 'say'.
'Are four minutes enough for you?' Rather than saying 'are enough', French uses a cognate of 'suffice' — literally 'four minutes, that suffices to you?'.
'Yes, that is more than enough.' Watch the word ahead of 'sufficient': it looks like 'largely', yet in French it means 'plenty' or 'more than enough'! Now let's listen to the whole dialogue again.
Qu'est-ce que tu fais là, Andréa?
Je dois te demander quelque chose.
On peut boire un verre ensemble?
Je devais absolument te le dire.

Stunned by Andrea's pregnancy revelation, Hicham grants her a few brief minutes before heading to London. Notice how the feminine adjective for 'pregnant' takes a silent final '-e'. See you next time!

source.show: Dix pour cent (Call My Agent!) S02E05

lines.fragment: Qu'est-ce que tu fais là ? Tu m'attendais ?
Je veux te demander quelque chose.
me séduire encore et m'embrasser encore
Tu es la seule personne à qui je devais vraiment le dire.
